passages.heading_path: INC-2288: Sustained CPU from an OS denial-analysis daemon > Summary
passages.text: A denial-analysis daemon held roughly 20% CPU sustained on mid-prod-f3 for six days, spiking to full utilisation during filesystem scans.
passages.cause_claimed: Denial volume from a policy change kept the OS denial-analysis daemon resident and busy.
passages.superseded_by: Platform security standard SEC-STD-14 (2026-01-30) requires the audit event dispatcher to remain active on production hosts. Deactivating it is no longer an available resolution, and doing it here destroyed the evidence that would have identified the source domain.

passages.heading_path: INC-2402: Newest change blamed first, later exonerated > Summary
passages.text: An investigation converged on the most recently deployed component within twenty minutes of the bridge opening. The component was demonstrated uninvolved the following morning, by which point five hours had been spent on it.

passages.heading_path: INC-2402: Newest change blamed first, later exonerated > Signature
passages.text: Detected under the stable signature `investigation.attribution:intg-prod-g2`.

passages.heading_path: INC-2402: Newest change blamed first, later exonerated > Timeline
passages.text:
- **D0, 17:20** Most recent deployment named as the probable cause on the bridge. No direct evidence recorded. Source: bridge.
- **D+1, 09:30** Component owner demonstrates the component is not loaded on the affected host. Source: bridge.
- **D+1, 10:00** Investigation restarts from the evidence that was available at 17:20 the previous day. Source: bridge.

passages.heading_path: INC-2402: Newest change blamed first, later exonerated > Resolution
passages.text: No resolution recorded for the attribution itself. The incident was closed with the cause unconfirmed.

passages.heading_path: INC-2402: Newest change blamed first, later exonerated > Gaps
passages.text: - Nobody recorded what evidence would have distinguished the named component from the alternatives, so the claim could not be tested at the time it was made.

passages.heading_path: INC-2411: Memory exhaustion on a batch integration host after a heap resize > Summary
passages.text: Batch transfers ran late on intg-prod-b2. The host was swapping heavily and the observability platform had opened and auto-closed a memory exhaustion problem on each of the two preceding days.
passages.cause_claimed: JVM maximum heap raised from 20 GiB to 28 GiB in a tuning change the previous evening, leaving no headroom for page cache.

passages.heading_path: INC-2411: Memory exhaustion on a batch integration host after a heap resize > Signature
passages.text: Detected under the stable signature `host.memory.exhaustion:intg-prod-b2`.
passages.cause_claimed: JVM maximum heap raised from 20 GiB to 28 GiB in a tuning change the previous evening, leaving no headroom for page cache.

passages.heading_path: INC-2411: Memory exhaustion on a batch integration host after a heap resize > Timeline
passages.text:
- **D-1, 19:40** JVM maximum heap raised from 20 GiB to 28 GiB under a standard tuning change, closed successful. Source: change registry.
- **D0, 02:10** First memory exhaustion problem opens and auto-closes. Source: observability platform.
- **D+2, 09:15** Batch transfers running late, ticket raised. Source: ITSM.
- **D+2, 10:02** Package and change history correlated. The heap change is the most recent change on the host. Source: bridge.
- **D+2, 11:30** Heap reverted to 20 GiB and the service restarted outside the batch window. Swap usage returns to zero. Source: host.
passages.cause_claimed: JVM maximum heap raised from 20 GiB to 28 GiB in a tuning change the previous evening, leaving no headroom for page cache.

passages.heading_path: INC-2411: Memory exhaustion on a batch integration host after a heap resize > Resolution
passages.text: Reverted the heap change and restarted the integration service outside the batch window. Confirmed by the swap curve returning to its pre-change baseline within the hour.
passages.cause_claimed: JVM maximum heap raised from 20 GiB to 28 GiB in a tuning change the previous evening, leaving no headroom for page cache.

passages.heading_path: INC-2411: Memory exhaustion on a batch integration host after a heap resize > Gaps
passages.text: - No process-level attribution was captured before the revert, so the contribution of any other consumer was never measured.
passages.cause_claimed: JVM maximum heap raised from 20 GiB to 28 GiB in a tuning change the previous evening, leaving no headroom for page cache.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: correlating change against onset > Run this first, not last
passages.text:
Package history and change records against the onset time is a lookup, not an
investigation. It costs one command and one registry query. It is routinely
run hours into a bridge, after the expensive hypotheses have already been
formed and defended.

Run it before the first hypothesis, so the board starts from what changed
rather than from what someone remembered.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: correlating change against onset > Correlation is not attribution
passages.text:
The most recent change on a host is the most available explanation, not the
most likely one. Availability is why the newest component gets named first,
and why it is often the one with a representative on the call.

A change that correlates in time earns a place on the hypothesis board with
its confidence stated and a falsifying test attached. It does not earn a
cause.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: correlating change against onset > Absence of change is not absence of change
passages.text:
Components that update themselves outside the package manager do not appear in
package history with a current timestamp. An empty result means the query
found nothing, which is not the same as nothing having happened.

Record the query, its window, and what it cannot see. A correlation report
that does not state its blind spots reads as complete when it is not.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: correlating change against onset > What to carry forward
passages.text:
For each correlated change: what changed, when, who implemented it, the
interval to onset, and the single piece of evidence that would rule it out.
The interval alone is not a ranking.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: collecting the security denial log > What this evidence settles
passages.text:
A denial log names the source domain of each denial. That is what separates
one candidate process from another when several are plausible and none has
been ruled out. Without it, every candidate stays equally likely and the
investigation converges on whichever party has someone available to answer.

It is usually a single command and a few seconds of host access. The cost of
collecting it is almost never the reason it goes uncollected.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: collecting the security denial log > Collect before suppressing
passages.text:
Deactivating the event dispatcher stops the denials reaching analysis, which
is often proposed as relief when a denial-analysis process is consuming CPU.

It also stops the log being collectable. If suppression is applied before the
log is taken, the evidence that would have identified the source is gone, and
no later collection recovers it. Collect first, then suppress if suppression
is still wanted.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: collecting the security denial log > Runtime changes revert on reboot
passages.text:
Setting the enforcement mode at runtime does not change the boot
configuration. The host will return to its configured mode on the next
restart, which may be months away and will not be associated with this
incident by anyone who was not on the call.

Any proposal to change enforcement mode must state whether it is runtime only,
and any record of it must say the same.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: collecting the security denial log > If the log cannot be produced
passages.text:
Record it as outstanding deciding evidence, name what each outcome would rule
in and rule out, and leave the hypothesis unresolved. A request that was made
twice and never satisfied is a finding about the investigation, and it belongs
in the record.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: host memory exhaustion > When this applies
passages.text:
A host is reported as memory exhausted, swapping, or showing an elevated page
fault rate. It applies whether or not an alert has fired, and whether or not
anyone has acknowledged one.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: host memory exhaustion > Establish the standing condition first
passages.text:
Find the resident set of the largest existing consumer and compare it against
total memory. A host that normally runs at ninety per cent of memory is not
the same incident as a host that normally runs at forty and has just moved.

The standing condition is not the cause. It is what decides whether a new
consumer of a given size is enough to matter. Record it as a condition, not as
a finding.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: host memory exhaustion > Attribute the memory before changing anything
passages.text:
Take a process-level snapshot while the host is still exhausted. Resident set
by process, ordered, with start times. A snapshot taken after a restart proves
nothing, and the restart is the most common way this evidence is destroyed.

If the snapshot cannot be taken, record that as a gap rather than proceeding
as though the attribution is known.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: host memory exhaustion > Distinguish a new consumer from a changed one
passages.text:
Two shapes present identically. Either a process that was not there before has
arrived, or an existing process has changed behaviour. The start time in the
process snapshot separates them, and they have nothing in common beyond the
symptom.

A new consumer points at change history. A changed consumer points at the
dependency or destination that changed underneath it.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: host memory exhaustion > What not to do
passages.text:
Do not raise a memory limit to relieve pressure before the consumer is
attributed. Raising a limit consumes the headroom that a correct attribution
would need, and it can convert an intermittent condition into a permanent one.

Do not restart the workload as a first step. It resolves the symptom and
destroys the evidence in the same action, which is how an incident gets closed
with the cause unconfirmed.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: selecting a recovery point during an incident > The window matters more than the age
passages.text:
A recovery point taken inside the affected window restores the condition along
with the host. The snapshot will restore cleanly, validate against every check
that does not look for the condition, and reproduce the incident.

Before selecting a point, establish when the condition began. If onset is not
known, treat every point after the first unexplained symptom as suspect.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: selecting a recovery point during an incident > Rehearsal is not validation
passages.text:
A restore that completes is not a restore that works. Time the restore, then
run the workload's own checks against the restored copy. A rehearsal that
stops at "the restore completed" has measured the storage layer and nothing
above it.

Record the elapsed time against the stated expectation. A restore that takes
significantly longer than the expectation is a finding whether or not the data
is correct.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: selecting a recovery point during an incident > What to record
passages.text:
The recovery point selected, the onset time it was checked against, the
elapsed restore time against the expectation, and what validation was run. A
rehearsal with no recorded validation is an untested assumption with a
timestamp on it.
